## 3. The changes where a deliberate prelude design differs from what the revival did, and the batch did not weigh it

**Strictly, I found none.** Each of the three deliberate prelude designs that differ from the revival's choice was weighed (P13 and P14, P16, P17). Two of them were weighed without the team commit that dates them as the team's later word. That is the evidence P-26 asks for:

1. **`fail` (P16).** The record weighs `fail(s: String): Zilch` as "the compiler prelude's own `fail`" and as "outside the specification" (`decisions-review/judgement.md`, section 2, option 3). It does not say that Steele made this change on purpose on 2011-06-13 (`0886e9654`). He replaced the generic `fail[\T extends Any\](s: String): T`, the shape that the one library keeps, deleted its "For now" comment, and added a return-type production to the grammar for it. Ground: L (a bottom result), and J (it avoids a JVM verify failure, row 447). What the revival did instead: the checker's instance rule (P-48, `f3032eed8`) and an unbounded `T` (`a1b5c253d`). That pair also clears row 447's verify failure at value positions, because the expected type fixes `T`.
2. **The order traits' self type (P17).** The record weighs the `comprises T` idiom (way 5). Its history of the idiom in the compiler's prelude ends at 2011-12-06 (`self-typed-bodies-ways.md:313`). It does not record that `StandardTotalOrder` was F-bounded, the one library's shape, until 2012-06-04. Steele first added `comprises T` (`655e65d53`, 2012-06-05). He then took the F-bound away (`59fdeff62`, 2012-06-06), in the same commit as a checker change for `comprises` clauses, which the record does cite for its checker half. So on the compiled path, the team's last edit of this trait went from the F-bound to the `comprises` idiom. Ground: L. What the revival did instead: P-146 reads `self` from the F-bound (`1c32ccffd`), and P-157 reads it in the exclusion test (`64fa505c4`). The library gains no clause.

The third design, `String`'s concatenation with `self` on the left (P13), was weighed by name. The batch rejected it because `1 || "a"` would fail (`rung-symbolic-library/REPORT.md:187`).

Prelude shapes that differ and were **not** weighed, none of them a design by the evidence:
- `Option` with `Condition` as its only parent (P10). The team's two drafts put `ZeroIndexed` under `Condition`, so the live shape is a bootstrap gap of the compiler world (J).
- `Generator`'s dotted `seq()` (P28). Its status is unclear. Steele's own documented form in `GenTest5` is `seq(self)`.
- `RR64`'s `^` at `RR64` and `ZZ32` (P6). Maessen called it a bootstrap state in 2009 (J).
- `GeneratorLibrary`'s parameter names (P24). This shape is the same as the revival's, not a difference.

## 4. The changes where the prelude has no counterpart, or only a stub

- **No counterpart:** every entry of section 2.3, and P20 (varargs; the code generator's limit, row 624).
- **Only a stub, with the stub's own words:**
  - the `case` guard's `GeneratorZZ32` (P19; "for now", "bogus", `525264af1`);
  - `Range` over `GeneratorZZ32` (P3; the same commit);
  - `ZZ32Vector` (P18, P21; a monomorphic vector for programs, `24717d4ad`, `d535963cb`);
  - `IntLiteral`'s throwing arithmetic (P2, `CB.fss:837`);
  - `String`'s `<` and `=` bodies `= false`, "(*) Needs to be replaced by generic definition once big operators work" (`CB.fss:372-373`), which no change in scope touches;
  - `Comparison` and `TotalComparison` without their order parents, "ought to be provided by ..." (P8, `CB.fss:1408`, `:1410`);
  - `TotalComparison` without `MIN` and `MAX` (P8);
  - `Option`'s single parent (P10);
  - `NonemptyReduction`, commented out (P25);
  - `SUFFIX_SUM`, commented out "For now" (`CL.fss:454`);
  - the `Matrix` stub (`CL.fsi:230`);
  - `RR64`'s `^` (P6).
- **The team's names for the prelude as a whole**, already on record: "stripped-down minimalist fortress library for first crack at compilation" (`c8d301411`); "bogus" (2009, `525264af1`, `ccccbe26f`); "bogo-trait" (2012, `b16964470`); "Hopefully temporary hack" (`compiler/WellKnownNames.java:109-111`). See `explorations/coordinator/two-libraries.md`, section 1.

## 5. What I could not find

- **Why the functional `seq(self)` is commented out** in the prelude's `Generator` (`CB.fsi:594`). The commit `e177c3e2c` gives no reason, and neither does any 2011-2012 message that I searched for `seq(`, "functional method" or "dotted" (section 8, command 4).
- **The authors of two lines** that first appear in parentless snapshots: `RR64`'s `|\self/|:RR64` (`9f63f9859`, 2012-04-09) and `Equality[\T\] comprises T` (`26718e298`, 2011-12-06). I did not compare tree to tree against a likely predecessor, as `bound-archaeology.md`, section 0, did for two other snapshots.
- **`CompilerBuiltinComparison.txt`.** The prelude's comment "Material not present for now. See CompilerBuiltinComparison.txt" (`CB.fss:1370`, Steele, `da5291587`, 2011-07-22) names a file that no commit holds (`git log --all --full-history -- '*CompilerBuiltinComparison*'` lists none).
- **The root `CompilerLibrary/` folder.** It holds ten api copies "used by BirdCount" (`21f9ebb01`, victorl, 2010-02-18), which no build reads (`rung-tabulate/SKEPTIC.md:50`). It is not in the brief's prelude, and I did not sweep it.
- **The transcripts.** I read the written record only. A batch may have weighed a prelude shape in a conversation that its records do not hold.
- **Kind 3 R1's 180 retyped sites.** I checked them against the prelude by type name only, not site by site. The prelude declares none of their types, apart from the `CMP` sites.
- **No measurement.** Section 2's column 5 is reading. The only measurements cited are the batches' own (`SkZilchFail`, `SkZilchLocal`, `SkCompiledLeft`).

## 6. Side findings

- **The audit's exclusion list is short by two commits.** `zero-audit.md`, B.1, "Excluded", lists the prelude commits `cee79d3f1` to `4ed46558d`, `6bec1b004` and `ce0c7f453`. Two more commits edit prelude files: `108ab82d6` (`GeneratorZZ32 extends Equality[\GeneratorZZ32\]`, and the bogus top-level `=` taken out, `CompilerLibrary.fsi` and `.fss`) and `031c38bbc` (`consume(): () throws IOException`, `CompilerBuiltin.fss`). `judgement.md`, 3.1, item 3, rules on both. Neither is a change of the one library, so the audit's count does not move.
- **A cast's exception kind differs between the two libraries.** The prelude has `object CastException extends UncheckedException` (`CL.fsi:83`). The one library's `cast` throws `CastError`, a `CheckedException` (`zero-audit.md`, A.4, row 352). The revival added about 50 casts (Part B, G4 and items 12 to 14). Once row 352's `throws` check is built, the prelude's kind would need no `throws` clause at those calls. No decision on record covers this.

## 7. For the record

- **Defects:** none measured.
- **Decisions:**
  1. My scope of (A): the commits whose recorded reason is the library, and `f3032eed8` with `fail`. Other way: every checker commit since the tag. No decision of the curator covers this.
  2. A prelude shape is a "design" in section 3 only where a commit or a text of the team gives it on purpose. Other way: every live prelude shape. No decision covers this.
- **For FACTS** (hand-over; the brief does not let me write FACTS):
  1. The fact: the prelude's `fail(s: String): Zilch` is Steele's deliberate replacement of `fail[\T extends Any\](s: String): T` (`0886e9654`, 2011-06-13, "Added type None to parser for return types"; renamed `Zilch` in `a62b3f3a4`). What it means: P16's prelude way is the team's later word, not a stub. Shown by: `git show 0886e9654 -- Library/CompilerLibrary.fsi`. Detail: section 2.2, P16.
  2. The fact: in the compiler's prelude, `StandardTotalOrder` lost its F-bound for `comprises T` on 2012-06-05 and 2012-06-06 (`655e65d53`, `59fdeff62`, both Steele). What it means: the history of the self-type idiom that P-146 rests on misses the team's last edit of that trait. Shown by: `git show 59fdeff62 -- Library/CompilerAlgebra.fsi`. Detail: section 2.2, P17.
- **Questions for the curator:** none taken by me. Section 3 gives the two weighed items whose dated evidence is new to the record. Whether either goes back to the curator is the judge's call.
- **Commands:** section 8.

       P=PATH; S=REGEX; prev="(none)"
       git log --all --full-history --format='%ct %h %an %ad %p|%s' --date=short -- "$P" | sort -n -u |

A rule is cited by its bracketed name, as the sources print it (`\infrule[Meet-Third]`), and by file and line; a figure or theorem also by its `\label`. The paper's calculus is FGFV, "Featherweight Generic Fortress with Variance". P-26 counts the paper and its report as the team's last word and work, and F-271 records what its proof leaves out.

**The code.** Lines are on `main` at `501140f96`, whose code is that of `c040df488` (only `explorations/coordinator/BOOT.md` changed between them). `scala_src/` stands for `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/`, `compiler/` for `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/` and `interpreter/` for `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/`. ## Findings: departures with no row and no decision

Each is by reading; none was run. Each gives the rule, the code, what follows, and what would settle it.

1. **The exclusion test reads every static parameter as invariant.**
   - *Rule.* Constructability of a common subtype (`appendix.tex:203-206`): at a covariant parameter two instances cannot have one only where their arguments exclude; at a contravariant one, never. [Anc-Same-Trait] (`lang.tex:393-397`) admits two instances of a covariant trait where a third below both is an ancestor too.
   - *Code.* `checkP` (`scala_src/types/TypeAnalyzer.scala:541-555`) excludes wherever an argument pair is not equivalent (`:547-551`), while the subtype test reads the declared variance (`:274-280`).
   - *What follows*, only under `covariant` or `contravariant` (P-62's future work; row 404 holds the run-time half): under `trait C[\covariant S\]` with `trait Dog extends Animal` and `trait Cat extends Animal`, neither excluding the other, the hierarchy check refuses `object D extends { C[\Dog\], C[\Animal\] }`, which the rule admits; and the overloading check accepts `f(x: C[\Dog\])` beside `f(x: C[\Cat\])` as excluding, though `object DC extends C[\DogCat\]`, with `trait DogCat extends { Dog, Cat }`, is below both, so `f(DC)` has no most specific declaration. ## Questions for the curator: decisions not taken

Each sets a rule of the paper beside a decision of his that it disagrees with. The paper is the team's last word (P-26; POPL 2019, with its technical report). Where the record has weighed the point before, the place is named.

### Question 1. Row 786: is the meet of two generic declarations empty where their parameters' bounds exclude?

- **The question.** `tint[\T extends Red\](x: Box[\T\])` beside `tint[\T extends Blue\](x: Box[\T\])`, the three objects: valid (walk) or refused (the checker)?
- **The rule.** [Meet-Excl] through existential reduction, which collects "constraints C that make α different from Bottom" (`rules.tex:343-345`), with `unify` and `toBounds` named but given no rules (`rules.tex:252-258`). No instance is `Bottom` (`rules.tex:159`; `resolve.tex:239-241`, `:773-774`), and the reduction lemma assumes that the reduced bodies are not `Bottom` (`appendix.tex:1287`). By reading: the merged parameter's only instance would be `Bottom`, so the not-`Bottom` constraint cannot be met; if `unify` fails there, the meet stays unreduced and [Exc-Object-Same] over its two distinct parameters gives exclusion, so the pair is valid; if `unify` returns the merged parameter bounded by both, the meet is not shown below `Bottom` and the pair is refused. The rules state neither. The Working Draft left the same point open: "Do we want to consider only the exclusion between ground types or also the exclusion between the bounds of static parameters?" (`Specification-1.0-frozen/appendices/future.tex:265`).
- **The record.** P-48 says an instance is "never `Bottom`", for a call's type parameter. Row 786 (contested) reads P-26 as pointing to the checker's refusal; `fortress-repo` skill, `compiler.md`, "The checker's gaps": "No decision says which is right."
- **Ways.**
  - (a) *Valid.* The checker's reduction treats an existential whose parameter's bounds meet only at `Bottom` as empty, the rule row 786 names. The checker accepts such pairs and agrees with walk; the paper's ban on `Bottom` instances is read into the static test.
  - (b) *Refused.* Walk's `mayBeEqual` (`interpreter/evaluator/values/OverloadedFunction.java:1448-1472`), which today reads two type parameters as possibly one type only "unless their bounds exclude", would admit `Bottom` as their common argument, and walk would refuse the pair at load as the checker does.
- **Which keeps today's behaviour.** Neither alone: today the paths disagree.

- **The rule.** A pair whose domains overlap needs one declaration whose domain is equivalent to their meet (`rules.tex:57-61`), so every call has one most specific declaration statically (`rules.tex:509-524`).
- **The decision.** P-60: several declarations below both may together cover the meet through `comprises` clauses; a static call may have several most specific declarations, typed by the intersection of their return types, the declaration that runs unique only at run time.

  - (b) *The Working Draft's own plan*: identify the intersection of two closed traits with the union of their common subtypes (`Specification-1.0-frozen/appendices/future.tex:269`), so that one declaration is the meet and the theorem holds; the Meet Rule's reading of `comprises` changes and the intersection-typed calls go.

### Question 3. P-156's tuple rule against [M-Tuple-Trait]

## 0. The calculus against Fortress

- **Source.** `lang.tex:65-95` (`fig:grammar`), `:97-148`, `:224-236`; `intro.tex:203-204`; `related.tex:16-17`.
- **What FGFV has.** Traits with variance marks (`+`, `-`, `=`) and upper bounds on their type parameters; objects, always invariant, with fields; methods with type parameters that have lower and upper bounds (defaults `Bottom` and `Any`, `lang.tex:125-126`); expressions `x`, `self`, typed function values, calls, object creation with written type arguments `O⟦τ⟧(e)`, and method calls `e.m(e)` with no written type arguments. Union and intersection types and `Bottom` are internal types only (`lang.tex:236`, `:247-256`). Tuples are domain types, not values (`lang.tex:233-235`).
- **What FGFV leaves out**, which revived Fortress has: top-level functions, functional methods and closed types ("could be added back to FGFV in an obvious way", `intro.tex:203-204`), nominal exclusion and modularity (`related.tex:16-17`), tuples as values, coercion, `where` clauses, size parameters, self types, written static arguments at calls, the `override` modifier. The record reads Fortress's top-level functions and operators as the receiver-free case of FGFV's methods (`research/extracts/ParkPOPL2019-extract.md` §8).
- **What revived Fortress leaves out**, which FGFV has: declaration-site variance carried to run time (P-62; row 404), lower bounds on a method's type parameters (only the team's 2012 `dominates` clause, §4), union types at run time (§22).
- **So** each section below separates a departure from a rule (the code decides a case of the calculus otherwise) from an addition (the code decides a case that the calculus cannot express). Additions are named, not counted as departures.

## Part 1. Well-formedness

### 1. [T-Program]: a program's declarations have distinct names

- **Source.** `lang.tex:154-160` (`fig:wellformed`); prose `:261-277`.
- **Rule.** A program is well-formed when its class declarations have distinct names, each is well-formed, and its top-level expression types.
- **Example.** `trait Shape end` declared twice in one component is ill-formed.
- **Built at.** `scala_src/disambiguator/ExprDisambiguator.scala:790-792` ("Type ... is already declared."), beside the checks of top-level variables and functions (`:794-803`). The top-level expression is a component's `run()`.
- **Departs.** No. Components, apis and imports are additions (modularity). The team's table test of these refusals, `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/Compiled9.c.fss` with its 36 pinned messages, is gated as an expected failure (`compiler_tests/XXX9c.test`), so which of its messages the tree gives today is not established by reading.
- **Rows.** None found.
- **Decisions.** None.
- **Verdict.** Built.

### 2. [D-Trait] and [D-Object]: a class declaration and its visible methods

- **Source.** `lang.tex:166-181` ([D-Trait]), `:185-201` ([D-Object]); prose `:279-293`, `:418-422`.
- **Rule.** A trait or object is well-formed when its type parameters are distinct; its bounds and the types it extends are well-formed (§7); every pair of its proper ancestors satisfies the ancestor rules (§3); a trait does not extend itself; each method is well-formed (§5); and every pair of its *visible* methods, those it declares and those it inherits, satisfies the No Duplicates Rule, the Meet Rule and the Return Type Rule, the last in both directions (§17 to §19). An object also has distinct field names and well-formed field types.
- **Example.** The paper's opening case (p. 11:2; `explorations/reviews/popl2019-examples.md` A1): `trait A m(x: Number): ZZ32 = 1 end`, `trait B m(x: Number): ZZ32 = 2 end`, `object C extends { A, B } end`: `C` sees two `m` whose domains, read with their declaring traits as receivers, `(A, Number)` and `(B, Number)`, neither nest nor exclude, and `C` declares none at their meet, so the Meet Rule fails.
- **Built at.**
  - Acyclicity: `scala_src/typechecker/TypeHierarchyChecker.scala:195-201` ("... transitively extends itself.").
  - The overloading rules on each trait's and object's visible methods: `scala_src/typechecker/OverloadingChecker.scala:360-409`, dotted methods with the receiver's self type as the first element of the domain (`:208-218`). By reading, so does the paper: [R-Method] matches the receiver's ilk with the arguments' against the declaration's domain (`resolve.tex:176-180`), and `rules.tex:268-273` omits the class `C` of `d = (C, M)` only "for presentation brevity"; the Return Type Rule in both directions at `:515-516`.
  - Distinct field names: `ExprDisambiguator.scala:948-955` ("Field ... is already declared.").
- **Departs.** Two points.
  - *The visible set.* The paper's visible methods are those declared or inherited (`lang.tex:288-290`), with no hiding: a redeclaration at an inherited declaration's parameter types is a second visible declaration, more specific by its receiver, and the three rules judge every pair. The checker reads the traits chapter's inheritance instead: `scala_src/useful/STypesUtil.scala:1671` (`providedMethods`) and `:1683` (`providedAndOverridden`) leave out of the visible set an inherited declaration that a declaration of the type's own hides, and `OverloadingChecker.scala:702-731` checks the hidden pair's return types by the Return Type Rule (`:712-714`). So a hidden declaration meets no third declaration of the set under the Meet Rule. Whether this ever decides a set otherwise than the paper's reading of all pairs is not established.
  - *Distinct type parameters.* No check that a declaration's type parameters have distinct names was found by reading (finding 3).
- **Rows.** 650 and 653 (the `override` modifier: the code generator refuses it, the checker accepts one that overrides nothing).
- **Decisions.** P-147 (an object covers an inherited abstract method by several bodies) and P-149 (an abstract functional method from one trait and a body from a sibling): both decide cases that FGFV, which has no abstract methods, cannot state.
- **Verdict.** Departs (an addition on hiding; one premise not located).

### 3. [Anc-Diff-Trait] and [Anc-Same-Trait]: the ancestor rule

- **Source.** `lang.tex:388-397` (`fig:ancestors`); prose `:368-380`; history `resolve.tex:1047-1061` (the "Ancestor Meet Rule", Steele and Chase, 2012).
- **Rule.** Two proper ancestors of a class that are instances of different traits are always fine. Two instances `T⟦α⟧` and `T⟦η⟧` of one trait are fine only if the class also has an ancestor `T⟦γ⟧` below both. For an invariant parameter that forces `α ≡ η`: a class may not extend two different instantiations of one generic trait. For a covariant parameter it asks for an instance whose argument is below both; for a contravariant one, above both (extract §2).
- **Example.** `trait Tg[\nat n\] end`, `object Both extends { Tg[\3\], Tg[\4\] } end` is ill-formed.
- **Built at.** `TypeHierarchyChecker.scala:291-300` (two entries of an `extends` clause that exclude each other: "Types ... exclude each other. ... must not extend them.") and `:304-308` (a declaration that excludes a type it extends, which, by reading, catches two conflicting ancestors at any depth), both by the exclusion test's `checkP` (`scala_src/types/TypeAnalyzer.scala:541-555`), which counts two trait types as excluding where some pair of their ancestors has one constructor with static arguments that are not equivalent.
- **Departs.**
  - *Variance.* `checkP` compares every static argument by equivalence (`TypeAnalyzer.scala:547-551`), whatever the parameter's declared variance. So for `trait C[\covariant S\]` the checker refuses `object D extends { C[\Dog\], C[\Animal\] }`, which [Anc-Same-Trait] admits with `γ = Dog` when `Dog` extends `Animal`. By reading. Finding 1.
  - *Boolean arguments.* `checkP` reads no `bool` argument (`:546`, "Todo: Handle bool args"), so `object F extends { Flag[\true\], Flag[\false\] }` passes the checker (row 406).
- **Rows.** 402 (fixed: sizes compared), 406 (booleans), 416 (walk applies no instantiation exclusion).
- **Decisions.** P-43 (the exclusion rule stays, the numbers are flat), P-97 (the specification states it in Luchangco's two parts, examples that break it marked "Not allowed"), P-25 and F-166 (the 2012 Types chapter, which restates it with `covariant`), F-44 (the checker enforces it and its Return Type Rule relies on it), P-62 (variance is future work).
- **Verdict.** Departs (built at invariance, which is all that revived Fortress runs; the variance relaxation is not built).

### 4. [Binding-Empty] and [Binding-Step]: a method's type parameter bindings

- **Source.** `lang.tex:399-411` (`fig:ancestors`); prose `:437-446`; the reasons `resolve.tex:509-523`, `:1105-1112`.
- **Rule.** A method's type parameters have lower and upper bounds, and their bindings are well-formed when (1) a reference to a method type parameter falls to the right of its declaration, (2) no method type parameter occurs in any upper bound, only in lower bounds, and (3) each parameter's union of lower bounds is below its intersection of upper bounds. (1) lets dispatch solve the parameters in one right-to-left pass; (2) keeps that pass consistent (`resolve.tex:509-523`).
- **Example.** Outside the rule: `opr SUM[\T extends AdditiveGroup[\T\]\](g: Generator[\T\]): T` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:1993`) names `T` in its own upper bound. Inside it: `append[\P, Q\](x: SortedList[\P\], y: SortedList[\Q\])` with `P` a lower bound of `Q`, which Fortress cannot write (the paper's `append`, `resolve.tex:537-538`).
- **Built at.** Not in the checker, by reading:
  - Fortress's static parameters have upper bounds (`extends`). The team's grammar of 2012 also has a lower bound, `dominates`, one or the other per parameter (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/parser/NoNewlineHeader.rats:59-79`, `:320-332`); the specification does not state it. The checker reads it in the subtype test of one type variable against another (`TypeAnalyzer.scala:224-229`), in the inference of static arguments (`STypesUtil.scala:1028-1064`) and in the variance check (`scala_src/typechecker/VarianceChecker.scala:186-190`); the existential reduction keeps upper bounds only (§16).
  - Restriction (2) is not checked: F-bounded method parameters such as `SUM`'s type-check.
  - Restriction (1) is not checked by the checker, which binds a declaration's static parameters together (`scala_src/typechecker/staticenv/KindEnv.scala:40-51`; `TypeWellFormedChecker.scala:195-197`), so a bound may name a parameter declared after it. The code generator checks it only for a bound that is a bare static parameter: `compiler/OverloadSet.java:1501-1515` ("Bad Scoping of static parameters found during runtime inference codegen"), which reads `Y extends X`, a bound that (2) forbids, as a lower bound on the earlier `X`, the dual of the paper's orientation. Finding 5.
  - Restriction (3) has nothing to check without lower bounds.
- **Departs.** The checker accepts the library's F-bounded method parameters, which (2) excludes, so the paper's proof does not cover them (F-271). The judgement of 2026-10-23 bounds the risk: where an invariant argument position fixes the parameter, as `Generator[\T\]` does, the bound is checked and never solved, and microGPT's reductions are of that kind (`explorations/reviews/type-decisions-review/judgement.md` §5 (a)).
- **Rows.** None for (2) or (1). Row 677 (fixed) reads a `where` constraint as a bound.
- **Decisions.** F-271 (the proof leaves F-bounded functions out); P-78 (`SUM` and `PROD` are one generic reduction each over the algebra, which makes them F-bounded); P-146 (self-typed traits, whose F-bounds are trait parameters, which the rule admits); P-62 (variance, and with it the `dominates` road: `explorations/reviews/spec-refused-examples.md` item 3). The extract records "no decision yet" on the library's F-bounded functions (§8). Question 4.
- **Verdict.** Missing (no restriction of the rule is checked by the checker; the code generator checks part of (1)).

### 6. [Tc-Empty] to [Tc-Arrow-Return], flip and composition: variance of a type context

- **Source.** `lang.tex:466-534` (`fig:contextvar`); the premise in [D-Method] `:216`; prose `:448-464`, `:536-559`.
- **Rule.** Each position inside a type has a variance: the whole type is covariant; tuple elements, arrow results and a covariant trait argument keep the enclosing variance; arrow domains and a contravariant trait argument flip it; an object's arguments and an invariant trait argument are invariant. ### 16. Existential and universal reduction

- **Source.** `rules.tex:184-212`; prose `:309-356`, `:490-506`; `appendix.tex:1269-1321` (`lem:reductionpreserve`).
- **Rule.** Existential reduction simplifies `∃⟦K⟧α`: it collects the constraint under which `α` is not `Bottom`, conjoins the parameters' bounds, unifies, and gives `∃⟦K'⟧σα` with the solved parameters substituted and the others bounded by what the constraint leaves (`toBounds`, which can give lower bounds as well as upper ones). Where unification fails, the type stays as it is. Universal reduction applies it to an arrow's domain and substitutes in the result. Reduction is what makes instantiation exclusion close the gap between subtyping of domains and inclusion of applicable sets (`rules.tex:309-334`).
- **Example.** The `ArrayList`/`List` triple: the meet of the first two domains reduces to `∃⟦S extends T⟧ArrayList⟦S⟧`, which is the third's domain, so the set is valid (`rules.tex:314-334`).
- **Built at.** `TypeSchemaAnalyzer.scala:366-433` (`reduceED`): the not-`Bottom` constraint (`:398`), the upper bounds (`:384-389`), the unification (`:404`) and its check (`:418`), the new parameters (`:421`, `boundsSubstitution`, `:552-608`); `normalizeED` and `normalizeUA` (`:215-231`). ## Part 5. Dynamic dispatch

The dispatch rules are not the checker's: on the compiled path the code generator builds one dispatch method per overloaded name (`compiler/OverloadSet.java`), and walk chooses at each call (`interpreter/evaluator/values/OverloadedFunction.java:2194-2240`). The checker supplies their order (§20) and the static type of each call (§9).

### 20. [R-Method], [First-Dispatchable], [Topological-Sort]: the run-time choice

## 0. How to read this

- **The three layers**, his frame of 2026-10-26 05:25 UTC. L1, the language: the Working Draft (WD, the team's text of 2010-12, copied 2011-02-02), the revised specification, the papers of 2011, 2012 and 2019, the 2012 restart's Types chapter, the team's library as a statement of the language, and the team's later published word. L2, the team's implementation on the JVM: the compiled path's checker, code generator, class loader and run time, the compiler's prelude, and walk. L3, Java interoperability: how Fortress types and natives meet Java's. A ground in one layer does not by itself decide a question in another. Where a team text in L1 itself argues from L2 or L3 (as the 2011 paper argues from Java), the text is the team's L1 word and its argument is theirs to make; I count it as L1.
- **Verdicts.** *Holds*: the tenet is right and its sound reason exists in the right layer. *Holds, text*: right, but its entry states a weaker, misplaced or wrong reason, or lacks the reason the coordinator needs to weigh a trade-off. *Bends*: against a team text where the team left a way the revival did not take. *Reverse*. None of the nine is a bend or a reversal.
- **Consequential** is the coordinator skill's test: reverses, bends or reads anew a decision of his; touches microGPT; chooses where the three principles split or are silent; or cannot be undone. A ruling so marked is his; each carries a default.
- **Earlier judgements**: J0929 (`decisions-review/judgement.md`), R0929 (`popl-recheck.md`), J1023 (`type-decisions-review/judgement.md`), J1024 (`phase3-exit/judgement.md`). I do not repeat their rulings; section 6 lists where this review's evidence changes one.

## 1. In short

1. **His doubt is answered: no foundational decision was a mistake.** All nine tenets hold. Three were taken on incomplete or partly wrong information (P-42, P-43, P-37), and in each case the missing or corrected fact makes the decision stronger or leaves it unchanged. None weakens it.
2. **The layers were mixed in the record's reasons, not in his decisions.** Four entries state a reason in the wrong layer or with the wrong date: P-26's list of "later word" counts 2009 prelude code as later than 2010-2012 texts; P-43's "Why" calls the prelude "the team's last record of the Fortress way"; P-37 lets the one library "take a design of the prelude's" with no rule for when; P-42 says "the switch-over ends the departure" where one line of `Shell.java` does. One judgement of 2026-09-20 read a WD sentence (L1) as the reason to keep a compiled-path setting (L2); P-42 corrected the language rule nine days later, and the code change is still owed. The rewrites fix the reasons; no decision turns.
3. **The bound.** P-42 holds on L1 grounds now stronger than when he decided: POPL 2019 says `Any` in so many words; the WD's `Object` sentence is not in the 2008 text, enters in a 2009 bulk import, and the same WD section says type parameters take tuple and arrow types; the library instantiates at tuples; the 2012 Types chapter and Welterweight put tuples and `()` outside `Object`. Steele's 2012 commits implemented the WD's sentence on the compiled path ("amazingly, this was not yet implemented"), found it broke walk's tests, and confined it to the compiled path by a setting, inserting `extends Any` wherever the compiled libraries and tests needed tuples, arrows or `()`. That is enforcement of a written sentence on one path, not a choice of the language's rule; the team's later texts (Types 2012, POPL 2019) do not carry `Object`. The probe shows the compiled run time needs nothing for the switch: under `Any` tuple and arrow static arguments compile, load and run as they do with `extends Any` written; under `Object` the compile command silently miscompiles `id((3, 4))` as `id(3)` (row 691). Java interoperability points the same way: `java.lang.Object` is Fortress `Any` (`NamingCzar.java:447`). The bound is not a linchpin: only one line of `Shell.java` and ten test files rest on it.
4. **The prelude question.** A design of the compiler's prelude binds the one library when the team's later word on the language backs it, or when the team's text is silent or ambiguous and the team's own compiled checker enforces the design as a rule; a stub by the team's words, or an accommodation of a JVM or checker limit, does not bind; and "later" is a date, so a prelude line counts as later only if it is later than the library's text on the same shape and no later L1 text contradicts it. Under that rule the revival kept the interpreter library's text against a backed prelude design in exactly one place, row 816, reversed by P-158. The sweep's three dated designs do not bind: `fail(s: String): Zilch` (Steele 2011) is contradicted by the 2012 Types chapter and POPL 2019, which make `Bottom` inexpressible, and the revival's instance rule is POPL 2019's own; the order traits' `comprises T` (Steele 2012-06) spells a fact the checker now reads from the F-bound, and Naden's last word points to the bound-based form; `String`'s left-only concatenation has no team reason and the library's text and the specification's juxtaposition rule decide against it.
5. **Phase 3 closes with climb batch 22c**, which must carry four rungs: row 816's repair (P-158), row 782's nine operator headers with the export check reading operators (P-155 read to cover it), `List`'s two imports into the thirteen, and the bound `Any` for `fortress compile`. Its exit gate: the distance 0 over the thirteen, under the compile command's own setting, with operators and `abstract` read the team's way. Row 701, row 321, the 52 code-generator refusals and the natives are phase 4's. This moves the flip earlier than J1024 placed it.
6. **The rewrites** (section 5) are P-26, P-37, P-43, P-42, P-33, and smaller corrections to P-7, P-12, P-59, P-17/P-84, P-58. Each must make the coordinator weigh in the right layer, date "later" correctly, and know what the switch-over must run as well as check.

## 2. The nine tenets

### Tenet 1. The goal and its measure (P-7, P-8). Holds.

- **Sound reason and layer.** The goal joins two layers on purpose: the intent is judged in L1 (the specification as the revival revises it, the 2012 Types chapter beside it); the measure is L2 (microGPT compiled to JVM bytecode, running fast). The language itself states the aim: the WD is "designed for producing robust high-performance software" (`philosophy.tex:14-18`, `:33-35`). P-8 is a rule of weighing, his words, and lists "the implementations" among the designers' sources: right, so long as an implementation's word is read as L2 evidence.
- **Where the entry crosses layers.** P-7's second sentence, "where the team's later work, in the compiler or in the papers on types, contradicts the original text, the text is updated to follow that work", is his 10-12 words and is the mechanism of P-26. ## 5. POPL 2019: where the chain follows the paper, where it goes outside its proof, and which is a risk

**Follows the paper.** P-42 (the default bound `Any`, p. 11:9), P-45 and P-152 (Fig. 5, Fig. 6 and existential reduction), P-48 (the intersection of the upper bounds, never `Bottom`, pp. 11:19, 11:25), P-43's rule ([Anc-Same-Trait]), P-62's road ([D-Method]). Each confirmed in the recheck and unchanged since.

**Outside the paper's proof, a silence.** Functional methods, top-level functions, closed types and nominal exclusion are omitted and said to be addable "in an obvious way" (extract §1, §6); coercion, `nat` parameters, tuples and numbers are absent. P-146's body-half intersection is outside FGFV's syntax, inside the static checker only. P-156's tuple rule is outside the paper (no tuples) and against the Types chapter, a designers' text, not the paper. These are silences: the paper neither supports nor refuses them.

**Outside the paper's proof, a stated restriction, and so a bounded risk.** (a) F-bounded method parameters, the library's `SUM`, `PROD`, `BIG MAX` and every function over `T extends Integral[\T\]` (F-271): the restriction "no reference to a method type parameter appears in any of the upper bounds" protects the paper's one-pass right-to-left solve at run-time dispatch (p. 11:11). Where the parameter is fixed by an invariant argument position, `Generator[\T\]`, the bound is checked and never solved, so microGPT's reductions carry no risk; a generic reached only by dispatch with an F-bounded parameter not fixed by an argument would, in phase 5. (b) P-60's run-time uniqueness against Theorem 4.1: a stated theorem given up at calls between closed traits; its cost is code generation on intersection results (rows 540, 559) and it is recorded (`changes.tex:3521-3525`). (c) P-146's signature half avoided a third: Lemma 5.2's hypothesis that a declared type holds no type parameter inside an intersection (`ParkPOPL2019.txt:1098-1107`). The hypothesis is about matching ilks against declared types at dispatch, in phase 5; a self-typed trait's `X` is also fixed by its invariant receiver instance and by `other: X`, so matching has the parameter from other positions; the risk is real only for a dispatcher built as the paper's, which the compiled path does not yet have (row 538). Change 1 of section 4 touches none of this: the static exclusion test is not matching.

**Where he is "very wary to go against" the paper**: nothing in section 4's changes goes against a rule of the paper. Change 1(ii) is the paper's own reduction. Change 1(i) uses a fact the paper has no words for (self types) in a static test it does not model. The paper is silent on self types, on tuples as indices, on coercion and on the library; it does not decide P-156 or P-157 either way.

## 0. What the record knew, and what the paper says

The record's account (`literature.md` § 1) was right as far as it went: the paper keeps the invariant-instantiation exclusion through its ancestor rule, moves the return-type check to run time, and has no self types and no numeric tower. What it did not have, each checked in the text:

- The instance rule. "The Fortress team had assumed, because it seemed from several working examples to be in accord with intuition, that once the tightest possible upper and lower bounds for a method type parameter have been found, then the union (or pseudo-union) of the lower bounds should be chosen as the type to be used for that type parameter. We considered this and the hybrid technique ... but we were unable to complete the proofs of correctness of both the techniques. Since the minimum requirement for a type to instantiate a method type parameter is that it satisfies all the lower and upper bounds of the type parameter, the dynamic dispatch algorithm presented here always chooses the intersection of the upper bounds." (§ 5.4, p. 11:25, lines 1274-1284.) The rule itself is [Solve-Step] (§ 5.2.3, p. 11:19, lines 965-1016): the substitution for a parameter is the intersection of its computed upper bound and its declared upper bounds, checked against the lower bounds; "Because g' is a ground type, the solving step never instantiates method type parameters with Bottom."
- The static return type at run time. Dispatch "seeks the most specific method declaration with a dispatchable instance that is applicable to the ilk of the arguments and whose return type is a subtype of the annotated static return type" ([R-Method], § 5.2.1, p. 11:17, lines 888-896); "the language semantics needs to make the static types of method invocations available at run time" (§ 2.3, p. 11:7, lines 329-331). The upper bound of a return-only parameter comes from that static return type ([Dispatch], line 875: `g match ρ - bounds`).
- The default bound. "By default, each type parameter has an upper bound Any and a lower bound Bottom" (§ 3.2, p. 11:9, lines 418-419). `Bottom` "is intentionally not expressible in the surface syntax" (line 438).
- The overloading rules in checkable form (§ 4, Figure 5, p. 11:13, lines 630-661): No Duplicates as non-subtyping of domains either way; Meet as exclusion, subtyping or a third declaration whose domain is equivalent to the intersection ([Meet-Third], line 645); Return Type as one universal subtyping check, `arrow(d1) ⊑ ∀[κ,κ']((α ⊓ α') → ρ')` ([Return-Test], lines 656-660). Specificity is subtyping of existentially quantified domains, "a sound approximation of the subset relation of applicable sets, [but] not complete" (§ 4.2, p. 11:13, lines 673-675), narrowed by "existential reduction", which collects the constraints that keep a domain off `Bottom` and solves them (lines 733-743, Figure 6).
- A restriction the proof needs. A method's type parameter bindings are well formed only if "no reference to a method type parameter appears in any of the upper bounds" and every reference falls within a left-to-right scope; "restriction (1) makes dynamic dispatch more efficient and restriction (2) makes it consistent" (§ 3.3, p. 11:11, lines 565-570); the one-pass right-to-left solve depends on it (lines 1010-1016, 1258-1262). Trait type parameters carry no such restriction.
- What the calculus leaves out. "FGFV omits functional methods [Allen et al. 2007] and declarations of closed types [Allen et al. 2011], but these could be added back to FGFV in an obvious way" (§ 1, p. 11:3, lines 142-144); "FGFV does not support features like modularity, nominal exclusion, and closed types in their work, [but] they can be added in an obvious way" (§ 6, p. 11:25, lines 1302-1303). No coercion, no `nat` parameters, no numbers.
- The exclusion rule's form and date. [Anc-Same-Trait] (Figure 4, p. 11:11, lines 530-532): a class extending two instances of a trait must extend an instance below both; "the 'Ancestor Meet Rule' ... was introduced into Fortress in 2012 by Guy Steele and David Chase" (§ 5.4, p. 11:24, lines 1230-1232). For an invariant parameter only the same instance is below both; for a covariant one the lower instance is.
- Variance in full: marks `+ - =` on trait parameters, objects always invariant (§ 3.2, lines 406-409); a covariant parameter only in covariant positions, a contravariant one only in contravariant ones ([D-Method], § 3.3, pp. 11:11-12, lines 571-595); dispatch with variance marks (§ 5.2.2); exponential blowup only where union types meet contravariance, accepted (§ 5.4, lines 1239-1257); the two alternatives the team weighed in 2012, dropping contravariance or dropping union types.
- Cost. "In simple invariant cases, we expect the run-time cost to be relatively low but nonzero"; for variant cases "caching or dynamic recompilation" (§ 5.4, pp. 11:24-25, lines 1263-1273).

- **[Anc-Same-Trait]**: a class extending two instances of one trait extends an instance below both; blanket for an invariant parameter (p. 11:11; extract lines 68-79).
- **The static rules**: a generic declaration is "a single declaration whose domain type is existentially quantified over its type parameters" (p. 11:3); No Duplicates, Meet and Return Type over domains, specificity by subtyping of domains, "sound but not complete", narrowed by existential reduction, which collects the constraints that keep an intersected domain off `Bottom` (pp. 11:12-14; extract lines 136-160). Theorem 4.1: a unique most specific declaration for every call; "No Duplicates makes specificity antisymmetric" (p. 11:15; extract lines 161-164).
- **The run time**: ilks; every call carries its static return type (pp. 11:16-17); [Dispatch] matches the ilks against the domain, matches the static return type against the declared one, and solves by "taking the intersection of the upper bounds", declared and computed, never `Bottom` (pp. 11:17-19; extract lines 186-207). Completeness of matching "assumes that a matched type holds no `Bottom` and no type parameter inside a union or intersection", which every declared type meets (pp. 11:21-22; extract lines 256-260).
- **Left out**: functional methods, closed types, nominal exclusion, modularity, top-level functions (pp. 11:3, 11:25); self types, a numeric tower, coercion, `nat` parameters (extract lines 277-285; recheck line 21).

## 1. Fork 2's bound is an F-bound

**What carries it.** The half's commit `d3d31b5b2` writes the bound on two kinds of declaration:

- Traits and objects, 5 in the component and 2 in the api: `trait Vector[\T extends { Number, MultiplicativeRing[\T\] }, nat s0\]`, `object __DefaultVector[\...\]`, `trait Matrix[\...\]`, `object __DefaultMatrix[\...\]`, `object TransposedMatrix[\...\](mem: Matrix[\T,s1,s0\])` (`git show d3d31b5b2 -- Library/FortressLibrary.fss`, the five `+trait` and `+object` lines).
- Generic functions and operators, 32 in the component and 38 in the api: the factories `vector`, `tabulatedVector`, `matrix`, the products `pmul`, `DOT` and `juxtaposition`, the sums and differences `+` and `-` on the family, `squaredNorm`, the norm `||v||` (24 and 30), and the block's `+`, `-`, `MIN`, `MAX` (8 and 8).

**The trait-level bound is in the paper's admitted form.** [D-Trait] checks a trait parameter's bounds under the parameters themselves (p. 11:10), so `T extends MultiplicativeRing[\T\]` on `Vector` is well formed by the rule's form, as the library's twelve F-bounded traits are (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:73`, `:175-229`, `:265`, `:277`, `:446`, `:1341`, `:1508`, `:1516` at `HEAD`). The `nat` parameter beside it is outside the paper altogether.

**The function-level bound is outside the paper's theorem.** Restriction (2) excludes a method type parameter from every upper bound (p. 11:11). Fortress's top-level functions and operators are the paper's receiver-free case (extract lines 405-408, by reading), so `pmul[\T extends { Number, MultiplicativeRing[\T\] }, nat k\]` and the block's `opr +[\T extends { Number, AdditiveGroup[\T\] }, I\]` are Naden's rewrite shape, `add⟦X <: Ring⟦X⟧⟧(X, X): X`, which the extract notes the paper excludes (extract lines 348-349, 377-378). The api already holds 30 such declarations: `SUM`, `PROD`, `BIG MIN`, `BIG MAX`, `BIG MINMAX`, the four `BIG MIN_MIN` kin, `BIG BITXOR` (`.fsi:1973-2075`) and rung O's tuple orders (`.fsi:2633-2643`). The half adds 38. So the fork roughly doubles what stands outside Theorem 5.11, and adds no new kind of declaration. FACTS already says the theorem does not cover the library's F-bounded functions (FACTS, "The team's latest word on types ..."; recheck § 1.4).

**Same ground.** The restriction exists for the solve: a right-to-left pass that takes the intersection of ground upper bounds (p. 11:19), which an upper bound naming the parameter would not give. Where the ilk fixes the parameter at an invariant position, lower and upper bound coincide and the declared bound is a ground check after substitution, never a type to solve for; the recheck read this for `Generator[\T\]` (§ 1.4, "the bound is checked and never solved"). Every declaration of the family fixes `T` so: by a parameter `Vector[\T,k\]`, `Matrix[\T,n,m\]` or `Array[\T,I\]` (invariant), or, for the nullary factories `vector[\T,s0\]()` and `matrix[\T,s0,s1\]()`, by the result `Vector[\T,s0\]`, which the paper's second step reads off the call's static return type (p. 11:18) and the compiled path off the written static arguments. `additiveIdentity[\T extends AdditiveGroup[\T\]\](): T` (`.fss:3230`) is already that result-only shape. The judgement's own line holds: "the arrays' calls all fix `T`" (`array-fork2-judgement.md:173`).

**Dispatch and instantiation at run time.** The class loader stamps `Vector[\RR64,16\]` from the static arguments; the paper's run time has every type parameter "instantiated with ground types" (p. 11:17); the two agree. The dispatcher scans overloads most to least specific by the ilks, [R-Method]'s shape (p. 11:17; extract lines 180-185). Where the paper's instance and the value's differ, a parameter nothing fixes (recheck § 1.6), no array call arrives. The dispatcher does not yet carry the call's static return type (`OverloadSet.java:2048`), a phase 5 line already on PLAN; the arrays add nothing to it.

**[Anc-Same-Trait] and [D-Method].** The ancestor rule bears on the bound's satisfiers and the family's extenders, not on the bound: each number type extends `MultiplicativeRing` at itself once (`Integral[\I\] extends MultiplicativeRing[\I\]`, `.fsi:446`; `RR64` and `QQ` likewise), `TransposedMatrix[\T,s0,s1\]` extends `Matrix[\T,s0,s1\]` once, C4's `Diag` extends `Matrix[\RR64,s,s\]` once. [D-Method] constrains variant parameters' positions; Fortress's generics are invariant, so it is met trivially, and a bound is not a method position in the paper (it is checked by [D-Trait]). FACTS already draws the one consequence, that no self-typed algebra trait can be covariant (recheck § 1.1).

**Unsound, or outside?** Outside. The paper gives no counterexample for an F-bounded method parameter; it drops the shape so that its solve has ground bounds and its proof goes through (p. 11:11, p. 11:19; p. 11:25 on what it could not prove, which is the union-of-lower-bounds instance, not this). The library has stood on this ground since answer 7's `SUM` and `PROD` (`d846e3644`), on the 2011 rules as the checker implements them (recheck § 1.4).

**Verdict: stands, with a sentence.** The fork 2 judgement's § 2.4 and the record's sentence for fork 2 gain: the family's traits and objects carry the F-bound in the paper's admitted form; its 38 generic functions and operators join the library's F-bounded functions outside the 2019 theorem, each with `T` at an invariant position, where the bound is checked and never solved.

## 2. The block's per-operator bounds and "no blanket ring bound"

- The paper has no library, no numbers and no operators, so it says nothing on which capability a bound should name. The judgement's reading of POSITIONS, "The integration review's checks" (the letter bent on the two traits, the reason kept, the first half kept on the block; `array-fork2-judgement.md:100`, `:180`), is untouched.
- It sharpens one of the judgement's reasons for keeping `Number` (§ 2.5, "`Number`'s closure is doing work"). Each block operator is a pair of mirror declarations, `(Array[\T,I\], T)` and `(T, Array[\T,I\])` (`.fss:4756-4766` at `HEAD`). Neither is more specific, and no third covers their meet, so the Meet Rule holds only if the domains exclude ([Meet-Excl], p. 11:13). In FGFV two traits never exclude: it has no closed types and no nominal exclusion (pp. 11:3, 11:25). So the paper's own calculus would refuse the block. The checker proves the exclusion through `Number`'s `comprises` clause, the paper's existential reduction (pp. 11:13-14) run with the closed-type extension the paper calls obvious. That is why a bound on the block must keep `Number`: the ring alone (6c) lost the exclusion, and walk refused `MAX` at load with "at least one pair of parameters must have excluding types" (`array-fork2-judgement.md:110`).
- The same reduction over the closed family of 17 types is where row 688's minutes went (`perf-probes/checker-speed/REPORT.md` § 2, § 3). The paper's calculus never meets a closed family, so its silence on static cost is not evidence either way.
- **Verdict: stands, with a sentence.** The block's pairs are valid overloads through `Number`'s closure, which is outside FGFV; `Number` in each bound is what the Meet Rule needs, and the per-operator capability beside it is the paper's concern in no way.

That is walk's binding at dispatch (`IntNat.unifyStaticArg`, `array-fork3-judgement.md:46`) and what the opened call runs at. The judgement's promise, "within that function `n` becomes a static nat parameter", is the paper's instance rule at an invariant position.

The rule's warrant stays where the judgement put it: the 2011 Types paper's existential subtyping, both sides existential (`Papers/Types/fig-existential.tick:7-15`), and Welterweight's E-Sub. content.content:
Given type ${\tt T}\ob{X}$ where $X$ is covariant and type ${\tt S}\ob{Y}$ were $Y$ is covariant and for all $Z$
${\tt S}\ob{Z} <: {\tt T}\ob{Z}$. Let {\tt A} and {\tt B} be distinct ground types where ${\tt A} <: {\tt B}$.  If
$I <: {\tt S}\ob{B}$ and $I <: {\tt T}\ob{A}$, then $I <: {\tt S}\ob{A}$.
\end{quote}

With these two restrictions, we can prove that special case overloads involving covariant type parameters 
will now pass the return type rule as well (TODO).

\subsubsection{Exception for selfless types}

This restriction is problematic for expressing certain types of relationships such as the numeric hierarchy
that is expressed using the so called self-type idiom (now selfless types or trolls). Some sets of numbers
and the operators over them give rise to special algebraic properties known as rings and the more specialized fields.  Fortress
aims to support them in the following way:\\

$\begin{array}{l}
{\bf trait}~{\tt Ring}\ob{X <: {\tt Number}}~{\bf comprises}~X~\dots~{\bf end}\\
{\bf trait}~{\tt Field}\ob{X <: {\tt Number}}~{\bf comprises}~X~{\bf extends}~{\tt Ring}\ob{X}~\dots~{\bf end}
\end{array}$\\

The self-type idiom is realized with the {\bf comprises} clause which contains the instantiation of the self type.
The {\bf comprises} clause limits the types that can extend the given type to those appearing in the clause.
In this idiomatic usage, the type ${\tt Ring}\ob{X}$ is identified as $X$.  Thus a ${\tt Field}\ob{\mathbb{Q}}$
is really just $\mathbb{Q}$ itself.

Unfortunately, the numerical hierarchy contains crossed instantiations of the kind that we determined
must be outlawed:\\

$\begin{array}{l}
{\bf trait}~\mathbb{Q}~{\bf extends}~{\tt Field}\ob{\mathbb{Q}}~\ldots~{\bf end}\\
{\bf trait}~\mathbb{Z}~{\bf extends}~\{ \mathbb{Q}, {\tt Ring}\ob{\mathbb{Z}}\}~\ldots~{\bf end}\\
\end{array}$\\

A $\mathbb{Z}$ is a ${\tt Field}\ob{\mathbb{Q}}$ and a ${\tt Ring}\ob{\mathbb{Z}}$ but not
a ${\tt Field}\ob{\mathbb{Z}}$ which breaks our rule given above.  As above, we can come
up with an example that is unsound if we allow this type hierarchy.\\

$\begin{array}{l}
{\it add}\ob{X}({\tt Ring}\ob{X}, {\tt Ring}\ob{X}) :{\tt Ring}\ob{X}~(*){\it def1}\\
{\it add}\ob{Y}({\tt Field}\ob{Y},{\tt Field}\ob{Y}) : {\tt Field}\ob{Y}~(*){\it def2}\\
\end{array}$\\

Take type $\mathbb{Z}$ which is provided as the inputs to {\it add}.  Both {\it def1} and {\it def2}
are applicable.  But if we instantiate {\it def1}
at $\mathbb{Z}$, then we have a return type of ${\tt Ring}\ob{\mathbb{Z}}$ for the less specific
definition.  The more specific {\it def2} is only applicable when instantiated at $\mathbb{Q}$, but the
resulting return type ${\tt Field}\ob{\mathbb{Q}}$ is not a subtype of ${\tt Ring}\ob{\mathbb{Z}}$,
thus witnessing the failure of the return type rule.

Recall that the return type rule handles two failure cases: first, the possibility that more specific
type information at runtime will cause a more specific function definition to be chosen.  Second
is that the more specific function may not be visible to the compiler (hidden behind an API).  Note
that the first failure case should not actually apply here.  When we statically know that we have
a ${\tt Ring}\ob{\mathbb{Z}}$, we actually know much more than this.  The self-type idiom means
that this type is equivalent to $\mathbb{Z}$.  But $\mathbb{Z} <: \mathbb{Q} <: {\tt Field}\ob{\mathbb{Q}}$
which implies that based on static information {\it def2} should apply.  However, this does not extend to
the second failure case when the more specific definition is hidden.

One way to ensure that the first situation cannot happen is to rewrite the overload so that the self-type
is a bound rather than the parameter type:\\

$\begin{array}{l}
{\it add}\ob{X <:{\tt Ring}\ob{X}}(X,X) : X~(*){\it def1}\\
{\it add}\ob{Y <: {\tt Field}\ob{Y}}(Y,Y) : Y~(*){\it def2}\\
\end{array}$\\

This forces us to recognize the type ${\tt Ring}\ob{\mathbb{Z}}$ as $\mathbb{Z}$ in order for {\it def1} to
apply which will automatically also mean that {\it def2} applies.  This approach suggests further that
the self-type idiom should be more than simply an idiom and instead a separate construct which cannot
be used as a first class type, but instead only in bounds.  Victor and John have started working on this
sort of theory with their {\it trolls}.  However, the visibility problem shows that this is not sufficient to fix the
unsoundness problems with the cross instantiation.  Therefore, more work needs to be done in order
to understand how to best support the numerical hierarchy in the Fortress type system.

api CompilerAlgebra

  abstract opr CMP(self, other:T): TotalComparison

  opr =(self, other:T): Boolean

commit 655e65d530a2d8c259a3c5c792183c2d5eaba330
Author: Guy Steele <guy.steele@oracle.com>
Date:   Tue Jun 5 17:48:15 2012 -0400

    (1) Added dotted methods to trait String: indexOf, lastIndexOf, upto, beyond, backto, and before.  Added test library_tests/StringTest1.
    (2) Moved traits Comparison and TotalComparison from CompilerAlgebra to CompilerBuiltin.  Moved tests Comparison.test, ComparisonTest1, and ComparisonTest2 from not_working_library_tests to library_tests.
    (3) Added a new method makeSpecialArrowFromFunctionalMethod to STypesUtil, and changed OverloadingOracle.lteq to use it, so that when comparison functional methods to see which is more specific, the declaring trait will be taken into account.  (Using just the self type does not do the job, because it may be an intersection of the declaring trait and the comprises clause.)
    (4) Tickled the "Foo not in the trait table" bug again, so I augmented the patch in TraitTable to search not just CompilerBuiltin and CompilerLibrary but also CompilerAlgebra and GeneratorLibrary for missing traits.  Again, this is"just a temporary hack" until we solve the apiname problem.
    (5) Added BirdyLib/OPairs.fs[si]
    (6) Moved Compiled5.ad.fss and XXX5ad.test from compiler_tests to not_working_compiler_tests because this test blows up every time we add new overloadings to = and <.  This test has served its purpose and I propose to retire it for now, as we are constantly adding new data types to the Fortress libraries.
    (7) Moved other_compiler_tests/MaybeTest15.fss to not_working_compiler_tests; not sure why it now blows up, but gets a stack overflow when it runs, apparently in the method for opr = in TestJust (which calls "=" recursively, though on a different type).
